opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so when we started Databricks, the original vision was pretty focused. We came out of the AMPLab at Berkeley with Spark, and the initial product was essentially a hosted Spark environment with notebooks, aimed at data scientists who wanted to do large-scale analysis and machine learning without managing clusters themselves.

What we learned very quickly from early customers was that the data science part was actually not where most of their pain was. You'd go into a company and they'd say, "Great, we want to do machine learning," and then you'd ask, "Okay, where's your data?" And the answer was always complicated. The data was spread across a bunch of systems, it was messy, it wasn't reliable, and before anyone could build a model, someone had to spend months just getting the data into a usable shape.

So a lot of what our customers were actually doing on the platform was data engineering: ETL, cleaning data, building pipelines. And that told us two things. First, if you want to serve data scientists well, you have to solve the data problem underneath them. Second, the data engineering workload was in many ways bigger and stickier than the data science workload itself.

That pushed us toward things like Delta Lake. Customers were putting enormous amounts of data into cloud object stores, but those data lakes had no transactional guarantees. Jobs would fail halfway, you'd end up with corrupted or partial data, and there was no good way to handle updates, deletes, or schema changes. So we built a transactional layer on top of the data lake, and that turned out to be foundational.

And once you have reliable, well-structured data sitting in the lake, the next question customers asked was, "Why do I need to copy all of this into a separate data warehouse just to run SQL and BI?" That's where the lakehouse idea came from: one copy of the data, open formats, and you can do BI, SQL analytics, data engineering, and machine learning all on the same foundation.

So the big lesson was to listen to what customers are actually spending their time on, not just what they say they want to do. They told us they wanted AI. What they needed first was a reliable data platform. Following that pain is what took us from a data science tool to a much broader data and AI platform.

r001.rationale: The response says customers wanted machine learning or AI, but spent much of their time on the platform doing data engineering such as ETL, cleaning, and pipeline building.

r002.rationale: It explains that customer data was scattered, messy, and unreliable, and that teams had to spend months making it usable before building a model.

r003.rationale: The response identifies customers’ substantial data engineering work as a reason to address the underlying data problem, describing that shift as pushing Databricks toward foundational data platform capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, when we started Databricks in 2013, we were coming out of the AMPLab at Berkeley with Spark, and our view of the world was very much shaped by that. We thought the users were going to be data scientists and engineers writing Scala or Python, building sophisticated pipelines and machine learning models. That was the audience we knew, because that was who was using Spark in the open source community.

And the first thing we learned, fairly quickly, was that the people actually paying for the product had a much more mundane set of problems. They were not struggling with the algorithms. They were struggling with getting the data in one place, keeping it reliable, keeping it secure, and letting more than three people in the company use it. We would go into a customer and they would say, look, the model is great, but the pipeline breaks every other night, or the data in the lake is inconsistent with the data in the warehouse, and nobody trusts the numbers.

So that was the first lesson: the bottleneck is almost never the fancy part. It is the plumbing. That is really what pushed us toward Delta Lake, toward reliability and transactions on top of the data lake, because without that, nothing downstream mattered.

The second lesson was about who the users were. We kept seeing that for every data scientist in an organization, there were ten or a hundred analysts who only knew SQL, and they had no way to touch the data we were processing. The data scientists would do their work and then export results into a warehouse so other people could look at them. That was obviously wasteful, two copies of everything, two systems to govern. Customers kept asking us, why can't I just run SQL on this directly, with the performance I expect? And honestly, for a while we resisted, because we thought of ourselves as a Spark company, not a database company. But the demand was so consistent that we had to take it seriously. That is what became the lakehouse idea, and eventually Databricks SQL.

The third thing, which I think is underappreciated, is that enterprises care enormously about governance. Early on, when you are a startup selling to other startups, nobody asks about access control or lineage or auditing. The moment you sell to a bank or a pharmaceutical company, that is the first conversation, not the last. We learned that if you want to be the platform for the whole company, you have to solve those problems in a unified way, not bolt them on per tool.

So if I step back, the pattern was always the same. We came in with a technology-driven view of what the problem was, and the customers kept telling us the problem was broader and, frankly, more boring than we thought. Our job was to listen and expand the scope, while keeping the core idea that you should have one platform, with the data in an open format, rather than five systems glued together.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the founders’ expectation that customers would build data science and machine learning models with paying customers’ actual focus on pipelines, data reliability, and bringing data together.

r002.rationale: It says customers first needed data consolidated and reliable, and that without this “nothing downstream mattered,” including their models and analytics.

r003.rationale: The response says customers’ pipeline and data reliability problems pushed Databricks toward Delta Lake and broader platform capabilities, explaining the increased focus on data engineering needs.

astra-6.text:
What we learned was that data science was only one part of the problem. Before customers could do machine learning, they needed to get their data together, clean it, and build reliable pipelines. So helping the data scientist also meant helping the data engineer.

And customers wanted more people in the organization to use that same data, including analysts working in SQL. That pushed us toward a broader platform. The expansion came from following the customer’s workflow and understanding what needed to happen before—and after—the data science work.

r001.rationale: It says data science was only one part of the problem and that customers needed pipelines, but does not clearly contrast their aspiration to use Databricks for AI or data science with their actual use for data engineering.

r002.rationale: It explains that before customers could do machine learning, they needed to get their data together and build reliable pipelines.

r003.rationale: It says customers’ data engineering needs led Databricks to help data engineers as well as data scientists.

sol-6.1.text:
What we learned was that data science was only one part of the problem. A customer might want to build a machine learning model, but first they had to get the data together, clean it, and build reliable pipelines. So even when the initial conversation was with data scientists, a lot of the work—and a lot of the value—was in data engineering.

That pushed us to think about the whole workflow. Data engineers, data scientists, and analysts were working with the same data, but often in separate systems. The opportunity was to give those teams a common platform, so they could collaborate and take something from raw data all the way to a production application. That was a much broader need than simply making data scientists more productive.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts customers’ goal of building machine learning models with the data engineering work that accounted for much of their actual effort and value.

r002.rationale: It says customers first had to bring data together, clean it, and build reliable pipelines before they could build a model.

r003.rationale: It explains that the data engineering work led Databricks to broaden its focus to a shared platform serving data engineers alongside data scientists and analysts.
